title: Business secretary to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
description: Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expecte
body: Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change."If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk"."This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.JLR has not confirmed the scale of the job cuts, but said they would "simplify" the business and "improve efficiency and build greater resilience"."Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said."We will share further information with our colleagues first." It did not rule out the prospect of some compulsory redundancies as part of the plans.Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time."Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses.Reynolds was asked about the impact on the car industry of the UK's electric vehicle sales target, which means manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.He said one of the first things he had done as business secretary was give the industry more flexibility to work towards that and said there was a further consultation open on it."It's not where it needs to be and that's why we're willing to change the regulation to work with where consumer demand is and the industry," he added.He said he had also spoken with West Midlands mayor Richard Parker about supporting the business and its staff.JLR in July said fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be £1.9bn.In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about £1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.Additional reporting by Simon Jack

schema.headline: Business secretary to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected

title: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks
description: Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Str
body: Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz. The US military has denied the claim."The report came from Iranian state media and it's a total lie," said Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, according to the Associated Press.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued his own threats back at Iran, writing on social media on Saturday, "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, and that period of relative calm was shattered when the US resumed attacks last Sunday. Fighting has continued throughout the week, with the US launching multiple strikes on Iranian targets and Iran retaliating against US targets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.US President Donald Trump said this week that the renewed fighting would not last "too long", echoing comments both he and his administration have frequently made since the now six-month-long war began in February.  Months of negotiations between the US and Iran have not amounted to lasting peace, and there's little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon.The Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to the world's oil and gas industry, has been effectively closed since the war began, and has become a major source of leverage for Iran.Tehran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway.But Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.The conflict in the strait has led to an increase in  gas prices globally, and ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers.The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US hit $5.85 on Friday, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that an average of 9 million barrels of oil a day were passing through the strait, which could help ease pressure on energy prices.Wright told CNN with oil also moving through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows".In an interview with ABC This Week on Sunday, Wright added that gas prices should start to come down for Americans as summer demand begins to wane after Labor Day.

schema.headline: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks

title: England v Ireland: Sophia Dunkley cetury seals hosts' dominant series clean sweep
description: Third ODI, New Road, WorcesterEngland 291 (48.5 overs): Dunkley 119 (119); Murray 4-56Ireland 177 (44.2 overs): Hunter 39 (58); Filer 3-27England won
body: Third ODI, New Road, WorcesterEngland 291 (48.5 overs): Dunkley 119 (119); Murray 4-56Ireland 177 (44.2 overs): Hunter 39 (58); Filer 3-27England won by 114 runs; win series 3-0ScorecardSophia Dunkley's sparkling century led England to a comprehensive 114-run win in the third and final one-day international against Ireland at Worcester.Dunkley's run-a-ball 119 set up England's 291 before Ireland were bowled out for 177 in 44.2 overs, sealing a 3-0 clean sweep for Charlie Dean's side.England were eyeing a record total after opener Dunkley's second international century, but the innings fell away from 260-4 and they frustratingly lost their last six wickets for just 31 runs to be dismissed with seven balls unused. Dunkley added 73 for the first wicket with Maia Bouchier, who continued her fine run of form with 39, before Jodi Grewcock also wasted a good start as she was caught and bowled for 35 and Alice Capsey was unlucky to be run out backing up for 10.All-rounders Freya Kemp and Dani Gibson threatened to push England beyond 300 but it was the former's wicket that kickstarted the collapse as she was caught at long-on for 23 and a run of single-figure scores followed, though Gibson kicked on to an ODI-best 41. Leg-spinner Cara Murray was the pick of Ireland's bowlers with 4-56 as the visitors fought back admirably, and England only managed to hit seven boundaries after Dunkley's departure in the 36th over.Despite the disappointing end to the innings, England still had plenty on the board in another non-contest between bat and ball. Amy Hunter top-scored with 39 but no Irish batter was able to score at a strike-rate above 100 and the run-rate spiralled beyond their grasp, as Mady Villiers and Lauren Filer took three wickets apiece.The final match of the series concludes England's international summer. Their next confirmed games will come at the Champions Trophy in February, though a multi-format series against West Indies in the autumn and three ODIs against Sri Lanka are in the schedule, but the dates have not been released.This has been a series with an unusual context for England.Key stars such as Lauren Bell, Sophie Ecclestone and Nat Sciver-Brunt have been rested, which has presented opportunities to experiment with the likes of fringe players in Grewcock and Tilly Corteen-Coleman. But the curious cricketing calendar means they have few opportunities to play the format, with the autumn schedule still unconfirmed and their next home ODI coming in the Ashes next summer, meaning they have been simultaneously seeking stability.The opening partnership was one question that needed answering after Tammy Beaumont's retirement earlier this year, and a century apiece for Dunkley and Bouchier in this series has seen them take their chance.Of course, Ireland's bowling attack is incomparable to Australia's and to cite this as Ashes preparation would be very unrealistic, but England can only play the schedule they are given.Dunkley had been threatening in the first two games, falling for 73 at Leicester before she was stitched up by Bouchier's poor running at Derby - but she was not to be denied a third time.The 28-year-old started patiently, reaching her half-century off 63 balls after Bouchier dominated the strike early on, before kicking on and whacking her next fifty off just 37.A notable change to her game has been her improvement through the off-side, scoring her runs almost equally split across both sides of the wicket - a big change for a player previously known for her leg-side dominance.Ireland tested her with the short ball and forced her to hit to the sweepers, which she handled efficiently before her eventual downfall as she was brilliantly caught by Prendergast at deep square leg.Sciver-Brunt is likely to slot straight back in at number three, and England have a decision to make about whether Capsey keeps the gloves over Amy Jones, but for now, Dunkley and Bouchier have solved one of coach Charlotte Edwards' headaches.The series was also a valuable opportunity for England's crop of seamers to test themselves without Bell leading the attack, another area of their squad that needed strengthening. With spinners dominating the T20 World Cup earlier this summer, the likes of Filer and Issy Wong were sidelined, but both have stepped up admirably. Wong starred in the second ODI with her first international five-wicket haul before resting for this final game where Filer troubled the Irish batters throughout with her lively pace, which helped her take 3-27. Contrastingly, Ryana Macdonald-Gay offered a change of tempo with her niggly medium-pace and Edwards will be hoping for Kemp to return to bowling fitness soon in order to give herself another option in the middle overs alongside Gibson.Villiers took 3-33 with her off-spin as she claimed the big wickets of Hunter and Orla Prendergast, and with Corteen-Coleman waiting in Ecclestone's wings, England's bowling stocks are in a healthy position.Ireland barely threatened to reach their target, with captain Gaby Lewis falling early for 16 to dent their hopes almost immediately and fellow opener Alice Tector trudged to 29 off 59 balls, which saw the run-rate climb steadily.England were made to work hard for their wickets throughout a stalling middle-over phase but eventually they ripped through the lower order with Ireland's last five wickets falling in a heap for just 10 runs.

schema.headline: England v Ireland: Sophia Dunkley cetury seals hosts' dominant series clean sweep

title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
description: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian
body: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.Image source, ReutersBut fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".Figure caption, Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in KyivWitkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.Figure caption, Watch: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner say they are "encouraged" by Ukraine talks

schema.headline: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain

title: Anak Krakatau: Volcano eruption closes eight Indonesian airports
description: Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands
body: Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.According to local newspaper Kompas, several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents reported eye irritations from the ash, while some fishermen had cancelled fishing trips at sea similarly reporting sore eyes.One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told the outlet that he felt since Friday evening and it felt like "small grains of sand had gotten into my eyes", and that he needs to use eye drops to ease the irritation.The dust is so thick that he has to sweep the front yard of his house every five minutes, he also said.Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.The volcano - also known as Anak Krakatoa - collapsed in December 2018, triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.

schema.headline: Anak Krakatau: Volcano eruption closes eight Indonesian airports

title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
description: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.The proposal bei
body: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation. It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions. The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently."The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy."With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov. "Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as  repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk. Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee."This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.  Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside. "But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Photographer Natalia Mykhailenko switched even earlier. She has led tours of Odesa highlighting non-Russian elements of its history. These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists."We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage."In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said."Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world. Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian.""Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."You can hear more about the language controversy in  Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

schema.headline: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts

title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
description: Image source, RankinImage caption, Natalie Imbruglia is releasing her seventh album, Algorithm, on her own record label, LandgirlByMusic correspondent
body: Image source, RankinImage caption, Natalie Imbruglia is releasing her seventh album, Algorithm, on her own record label, LandgirlByMusic correspondentWhen it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion."I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says."If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing."So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause."It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness."I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger."You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The singer says she's dealt with stage fright throughout her life - but the anxiety was amplified by perimenopauseThings came to a head on tour, where her stage fright went into overdrive and she suffered "just terrible, terrible anxiety"."I become sensitive to sound, so it feels like you're screaming at me if you're talking normally," she says. "I can't process questions very well. I act twitchy and weird, and it seemed to get worse with perimenopause."She says her behaviour became a "nightmare" for her team. Pressed for an example, she explains: "If you asked me whether I wanted still or sparkling water, I'd say, 'That's a question, and I can't answer questions right now'. "How diva is that?"Well, it's not exactly Mariah Carey demanding baskets of puppies and forbidding eye contact, but Imbruglia was shaken up.The day after one concert, she told her co-writers David Sneddon and Anu Pillai, "Guys, I think I'm going to have to quit my job because I can't cope with how I'm treating people before the show."They helped to talk her down, putting her fight-or-flight instincts into context."What they helped me realise is that I was trying to stop the behaviour with willpower, and if I just relaxed into it and said to myself, 'You know, you're about to perform in front of a lot of people, it's natural that you're nervous', maybe I wouldn't be resisting it as much."The impromptu therapy session inspired a new song, Upside Down, external - but Imbruglia is understandably frustrated that perimenopause isn't more widely understood, saying many women are rejected by their GP when they seek HRT treatment."My mum never talked to me about it," she reflects, "but looking back, I know she had a really bad one."Her anxiety was off the charts, too, and I have a lot more compassion now, because she had four kids. I've only got one."Image source, Fremantle Media/ShutterstockImage caption, Imbruglia found fame as Beth Brennan in Aussie soap opera NeighboursAs a child in Sydney, Imbruglia was drawn to performing. She'd squeeze lemon on her hair to make it blonder, and put on concerts of Whitney Houston covers for her neighbours.Before long, she was cast in commercials for Coca-Cola and Twisties, and spent her Christmases singing carols in shopping centres."But when you turn 15 or 16, and you're into boys, you're like, 'Oh, that's really naff. I don't want to be doing that any more'," she laughs.From that point onwards, Imbruglia became "basically unparentable"."I was sneaking out and sleeping in someone's car on the beach, then getting busted."My parents were really strict - and my mum would turn up at parties with my picture, going, 'Have you seen this girl?' "Socially, it was a disaster."Music continued to be her solace. Dating a drummer, she switched allegiance from Whitney Houston to Tom Waits and Tori Amos, but the urge to sing remained.You can see that hunger in a recently rediscovered photograph of a pre-fame Imbruglia, external, pressed up against the barriers of an INXS concert in 1992."It was my first ever concert," she says. "I was 15. I had white, tight jeans on."In the photo, "everyone else is screaming but I'm looking at (Michael Hutchence) with this determination in my eyes."I'm studying him, like, 'How can I be up there too?'"Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The singer's debut album, Left of the Middle, was one of the biggest-sellers of the 1990sShe got her chance in 1997 after quitting her role as builder's apprentice Beth Brennan in Aussie soap Neighbours. Moving to London, she signed a deal with RCA Records and immediately scored an international hit with her first single, Torn.Famously, the song was a cover – a fact journalists never let her forget, even though she co-wrote every other track on her debut album, Left of the Middle (lifetime sales, seven million copies)."Yeah, I got famous on a song that I didn't write," she says now, "but there's more to what you bring to a song than whether you wrote the lyrics."She still loves the song – "Torn was a beautiful gift" – but the furore around it fuelled her insecurities.As a result, she essentially self-sabotaged her career. The lead single from her second album, That Day, was a free-verse stream-of-consciousness that sounded like a manic inner monologue."That was my rebellion against Torn," she says. "It doesn't have a chorus. "That was my way of going, 'Can I get on with my life now? I've just started learning the craft of songwriting, I'm young, I didn't ask for this'."Image source, RankinImage caption, Imbruglia became a mother in 2019 and her son's name, Max Valentine, is tattooed on her left armIn the midst of the madness, she auditioned for the lead role of Satine in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge – which counts as one of the stranger experiences of her career."The audition was, pretty much, 'Have an orgasm'," she grimaces. "Because I think that happens in the movie." (Indeed, Satine delivers a breathy boudoir monologue, external as she tries to seduce Ewan McGregor's character, Christian.)But Imbruglia stresses it wasn't a creepy casting couch situation."It's Baz, that doesn't really fit," she says of the  soft-hearted director."But I remember leaving and feeling really icky. Like, 'Ohhh, that was awful. Where's my mummy?'"Back in the world of music, Imbruglia returned to more commercial sounds on hits like Wrong Impression (2002) and Shiver (2005). But sales dwindled and her fourth album was shelved by her label.In the years that followed, she joined the Australian version of The X Factor and appeared in a UK production of Alan Ayckbourn's play Things We Do for Love, before making a tentative return to music with covers album Male (2015); and the more personal, introspective Firebird (2021)."It was quitting music and coming back to it that gave me an appreciation of my abilities," she says."I might not be the best songwriter, even now, but there's only one me, and when I go inside myself and feel the emotion of what I'm writing about and deliver it, that's what my fans resonate with, and that's enough."Image source, Natalie Imbruglia / LandgirlImage caption, She shot the video for her latest single, Beautiful Love, on her iPhone, and it features the Mercedes she bought with the proceeds of her first album in 1997She certainly has a lot to say on Algorithm. As well as the frank discussion of mental health, the title track talks about her flirtation with internet conspiracy theories.She won't say which ones ("I think it's irresponsible") but stresses the danger is omnipresent."There's a voice in my head that says, 'You don't want to click on that', and I'll click on it. It's like this compulsion."You have to change the settings. Don't allow yourself to be in a situation where your stress relief is scrolling on a phone in bed. It's just not healthy."Ultimately, however, the album ends on a note of positivity. Beautiful Love, external, co-written with Snow Patrol's Gary Lightbody, is a soaring hymn to embracing your flaws and making peace with life's highs and lows."I've always made the joke that I'll never be a Buddhist because it's a middle path," she smiles."I like the pendulum to swing. Whether it's extreme joy or extreme pain, I like to feel the experience of life."

schema.headline: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'

title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
description: Image source, Halfpoint ImagesByGrace Dean and Mallory Moench"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental
body: Image source, Halfpoint ImagesByGrace Dean and Mallory Moench"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September."It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day. "If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."Image source, Stacie MatthiasImage caption, Stacie says she always has something to "remember, organise or worry about"In a survey looking into the mental load that involved 3,000 US parents, academics at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne , externalfound that mothers handled 71% of household tasks that required mental effort, such as keeping track of when sheets and towels needed to be washed and remembering by when food in the fridge needed to be eaten.The study found that fathers handled many of the tasks researchers described as "episodic" - things that happen less often, such as remembering when to get the car serviced.University of Melbourne Prof Leah Ruppaner describes the mental load as being invisible, enduring and without boundaries. "You don't bring your dishes to work, but you bring the mental load everywhere," she says.The mental load is a popular topic on forums like Reddit and Mumsnet, where women seek advice about how to talk to their partners about the exhaustion of trying to juggle so many different responsibilities.Mums told BBC News they were often added to school WhatsApp groups - where parents discuss things like non-uniform days, school trips, birthdays and lost property - as the "default parent", while their partners never joined.Sophia, a 35-year-old mum of three in Portsmouth, pays for school trips and makes lunch orders on her children's school's app on her phone, but says her husband has never downloaded it.Sophia says she tried multiple times to explain the concept of the mental load to her husband - but feels he didn't understand and dismissed her concerns as "quick tasks"."They are quick tasks if you could just do the task," Sophia says, "but I have to plan for the task, I have to anticipate the task, I have to be 10 steps ahead all the time."Image source, Getty ImagesSam Berry, a deputy headteacher, content creator and married dad of two in London, says when his wife first raised the idea of mental load after his eldest was born, he "didn't really get it" and was "a bit defensive" because he thought he was doing a lot - changing nappies, feeding the baby and more.He would ask what he could do to help, but he says that still puts the burden on the other person to do the thinking.As Stacie explains: "I always say to my partner: 'If I have to ask you to do something, that's just adding to my mental load'."It took a few months of talking and listening for Sam to understand that it was not only about completing the task, but the thinking around it - not just cooking dinner, but what food was in the house, planning the meal, and doing the shopping.Clinical psychologist Natasha Wallace says some women come to her feeling stressed by the pressure they feel to organise their households."It's often, for them, not one enormous stressor," she says. "It's when they realise that they have hundreds of tiny demands on them and their brains and bodies just can't switch off."Many women are running on autopilot, she adds, so they often don't realise the extent of the cognitive load they're carrying, and this constant low-level stress can have an effect on the nervous system. In turn, this can cause poor sleep, irritability and decision fatigue, she says.Image source, Natasha WallaceImage caption, Wallace says being constantly stressed can impact mental health and restAnita Cleare, parenting expert and author of The Work/Parent Switch, said the overall cognitive drain spills over into our work lives and leads to unsustainable burnout.One piece of research found , externalthat men who earned more did less physical and cognitive labour related to the household, but that when women's earnings increase, they do less physical housework but still the same amount of cognitive labour.Women very seldomly feel it is a choice to opt out of family life, so the choice then becomes whether to decelerate their career, go part-time, or stop and stay home - with more and more women making that decision, Cleare says."If you lower the domestic load, if you lower the mental load, you will create energy, capacity, interest in being able to perform more and better at work."Why the disparity?Many of the women the BBC interviewed said they believed the disparity began with maternity leave.Wallace says that because women typically take much longer for maternity leave than dads do for paternity leave, they become the "default parent" very early on."If you become the person who knows everything, knows where everything is and has in the past done everything, everybody starts coming to you for everything," she says, "so you remain that central person even if you return to work."In the UK, mothers can take up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, 39 of which can be paid, while fathers can take up to two weeks of leave with statutory paternity pay. Parents can also take shared parental leave.Some employers offer extra parental leave to their workers, but most people earn less when on maternity or paternity leave, which affects how much leave many fathers take.Cleare says workplaces can help by making examples of fathers taking paternity leave, not just offering it, and by setting expectations around when employees are contactable, and supporting career conversations for women.It can also come down to what are seen as traditional roles.Zach Watson, a married father of three and coach in the US on sharing the mental load, says his grandfather might never have cooked a meal in his married life, while his father did only a little.In the first five years of his marriage, his wife cooked most of the time. If he offered to cook, he would ask her what she wanted - a question that could actually add to her mental load.He learned he could come to her with options for dinner, having already looked in the fridge, and give her a default if she wanted to opt entirely out of decision-making. And if he needed help, instead of just asking "Where's the ketchup?", he could explain where he had already looked.Image source, Maskot/Getty ImagesImage caption, Women say it's crucial that their partners take full ownership of their tasksSam Berry says while some men do not care, a big group - his audience online - "actually are really good husbands, are really good dads, they are trying their best and want to do the best they can, but almost haven't seen it or don't have the language".Many women the BBC spoke to were keen for their partners to take ownership of certain tasks.Sam calls this taking on "a category of tasks" - so dad might handle all the school admin, while mum manages the food.However, he says equality is not necessarily about splitting everything 50/50 - because one partner might work more and another might like cooking - but about finding what works best for both partners.And if you traditionally hold more of the mental load, you might need to accept that your partner may do things very differently, and it might not always go smoothly, says Afua Williams, 40, a mother of two in London.Image source, Afua WilliamsImage caption, Afua Williams says she always has a lot to think about come SeptemberHow to lighten the loadThose who spoke to BBC News shared their own tips about how to manage the mental load equally:Communicate clearly with your partner about how you're feeling and the impact of your mental load. Zach calls it "labelling" - making the invisible cognitive and emotional labour visible. Don't have these conversations when you're feeling angry or overwhelmed, says Wallace, or it can feel like the other person is being "blamed or criticised""See what you can offload", says Ana Catalano Weeks, co-author of a study , externalon how mental load impacts work. Do you really need to organise physical birthday cards for your children's friends? Can you mute parents' WhatsApp groups and just focus on official school emails?Have regular check-ins with your partner - it could be daily, weekly, or seasonallyCreate a shared calendar so that everyone is aware of birthdays, school meetings and moreTake ownership of tasks from start to finish without the need to be reminded, Wallace saysDon't fall into the "efficiency trap" that the solution is just to be more organised, Cleare says. Remember that what matters most as a parent are moments of connection with your child - not eating certain vegetables - and that will help redefine expectations

schema.headline: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it

title: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi
description: Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed. One told news agency ANI that the other building had also be
body: Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed. One told news agency ANI that the other building had also been a hostel.Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure"."Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added.Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old.The owner of a nearby shop told ANI that it had been under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to expand the hostel and increase their income."They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak," he said, noting that the construction workers had also been buried.The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account."Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said.Police are searching for the owner of the building, Times of India reports.Satya Niketan is a densely populated area which houses a large student population, with a number of hostels in the neighbourhood.Building collapses are relatively common in Delhi, with more than a thousand recorded in the past three years causing dozens of deaths, according to fire department figures. Poor foundations, inadequate materials and unqualified construction workers were among the common reasons for collapses.Eleven people, including three children, were reportedly killed last April when a residential building collapsed in north-eastern Delhi.

schema.headline: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi

title: Raise the Colours founder Ryan Bridge charged with 14 offences
description: The founder of an activist group which has been putting Union Jack and St George's Cross flags on lampposts has been charged with a string of offences
body: The founder of an activist group which has been putting Union Jack and St George's Cross flags on lampposts has been charged with a string of offences including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behaviour and assault.Ryan Bridge, 45, of Blackwell, Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, has been erecting flags in the Midlands and the south of England since last summer as part of Raise the Colours.Thames Valley Police said Bridge had been charged with 14 offences from a two-month period in Oxfordshire earlier this year. He is due to appear at Oxford Magistrates' Court on 3 November.The offences are: Seven counts of using threatening words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distressThree counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violenceTwo counts of racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distressOne count of racially aggravated fear of violenceOne count of common assaultIn July, Oxfordshire County Council was granted a High Court injunction to stop people placing flags near highways because of safety concerns, trespass and obstruction. Birmingham City Council has applied for a similar injunction which will be heard at the High Court on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Raise the Colours founder Ryan Bridge charged with 14 offences

title: Jamaican officials to bring reparations petition to King Charles
description: The Jamaican government will hand a petition to King Charles over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said
body: The Jamaican government will hand a petition to King Charles over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC.King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral.Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."When slavery was abolished across most of the empire in 1833, the British government paid £20m to slave owners in compensation. The loans taken out to raise the money were paid off in 2015.Grange said: "Up to 2015, Britain was paying the slave masters, because we were being considered property."The question really should be: if in modern times we're still paying back the slave masters for the property that was our people, our ancestors, for property that was because of the abolition of slavery, then why shouldn't we be pursuing some remedy at this time?"Grange will also meet with British Museum officials to "advance discussions on the repatriation of artefacts" taken from Jamaica during the colonial era.She said: "They are priceless, they are significant to the story of Jamaica and we are working to bring them home."In 2015, David Cameron, who was prime minister at the time, ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade, while visiting Jamaica.Speaking to MPs in Jamaica's parliament, Cameron said slavery was "abhorrent in all its forms". He added that he hoped they could "move on from this painful legacy and continue to build for the future".

schema.headline: Jamaican officials to bring reparations petition to King Charles

title: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority
description: Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, accord
body: Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, according to incomplete results. Projections indicate it is set to fall short of a majority, but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.The far-right AfD is set to win a record 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on just over 17%.The AfD's charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible.No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.With more than 90% votes in, the AfD is set to score higher than earlier opinion polls suggested, and Siegmund along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as the news emerged. Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant."This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.The AfD's leaders will not know if they have enough seats to govern until they see which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament. Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, but the party's national leaders see it as a possibility. "If necessary there'll just be new elections, then we'd just get 50 or 55%," said Siegmund, while saying he was prepared to work with individual MPs or a party.A big question-mark hangs over whether one populist left-wing party, BSW, gets over the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament. If BSW fails, then the AfD's chances of a majority increase. If they get in, the AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament.A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem."We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory and said his party would have to deal with the result: "This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign."Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it.AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland and it openly pro-Russia and anti-migration.  It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result as well. Although the outcome was initially unclear, the party's supporters believe they are on the march.Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at an estimated 78%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters.One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give.""No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC.Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more."Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states.But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis.Nikita, a demonstrator at an anti-AfD "Democracy Festival" in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote said Germans had to "learn from our history and not go back. We don't want the dark times any more".Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline".One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".

schema.headline: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority

title: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners
description: Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.Former Ma
body: Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.Former Manchester City goalscorer Julian Alvarez was on their radar but remains at Atletico Madrid, while the Gunners were also interested in Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Vinicius Jr.While Rogers opted for London rivals Chelsea, Barcola moved to Liverpool and Vinicius Jr has stayed at Real Madrid.Yet reigning champions Arsenal have started this season as strongly as they finished 2025-26, when they celebrated their first Premier League title for 22 years.After wins over Coventry City and Aston Villa, they came from behind to beat big-spending Chelsea 2-1 in a thrilling derby on Sunday - thanks to goals from two familiar faces.Kai Havertz, an Arsenal player since 2023, and Martin Odegaard, who joined in 2021, scored as they passed their first big test of the campaign against opponents who have spent close to £350m since the end of last season.A maximum nine points from three games, one goal conceded and big players stepping up."I can't see anyone stopping Arsenal," former Premier League winner Chris Sutton told BBC Sport.It is surely too early in the season to get carried away, and there are likely to be bigger tests ahead for Mikel Arteta's side.But Arsenal have set down an early marker as they chase back-to-back Premier League crowns.Along with Manchester City, they are one of only two clubs with a maximum nine points from three games.After sweeping aside Coventry on the opening day of the season, they produced a mature performance to come away with all three points at Villa.Against Chelsea, they had to find a different way to win after £117m signing Rogers fired Chelsea into a second-minute lead."Our mentality is to keep fighting. We have shown that many times," said captain Odegaard, who scored the 50th-minute winner after Havertz had equalised before half-time."We never want to concede early, but the reaction is top. We got our reward in the end and the response was brilliant."We showed our quality with and without the ball and the result reflects that."Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances in all competitions this season, after netting only once in 36 last term."It was a big game, massive game, tough opponent, and we got there in the end, so brilliant," he said.Former Manchester United and England player Ashley Young said Odegaard's form will be key for Arsenal this season."He's just a joy to watch," Young told BBC Sport."He's exciting when he gets on the ball, he's allowing other players to get on the ball."The connection down the right side between him, Bukayo Saka and Havertz - it's just good to see when you've got players that know each other and build relationships in that way."Riccardo Calafiori has been brilliant from last season. He seems to me like he's the one that's got a free role in the team."It was his run, and he played it precisely, for the winning goal. He goes quickly, takes people out of the way. It's just clever. Arsenal deserved all three points."Havertz said Odegaard was back to his "very best"."He's an unbelievable player - we have seen that over the last years," said the Germany forward."He's going to help us a lot this season."Sutton said Arsenal are still ahead of the rest, despite their rivals spending hundreds of millions of pounds during the transfer window."They're such a powerhouse," said the former Blackburn and England striker."Chelsea are a good team, but Arsenal always find a way to win. Can you stop Arsenal? I don't think they [other Premier League teams] can."Arsenal have won their opening three games of a top-flight campaign while conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time - after 1924-25, when they finished 20th, and 2003-04, when they went the season unbeaten.They have also won eight league games in a row stretching back to last season.Having seen off big-spending Chelsea, their next league match is at Sunderland on Saturday.Before that Arsenal launch their Champions League campaign at Napoli on Wednesday.Havertz said Arsenal will head to Italy with confidence high with after seeing off his former club Chelsea."Chelsea have an amazing squad, but so do we," said Havertz, who scored the winning goal for the Blues against Manchester City in the 2021 Champions League final."We knew it was going to be tough. They scored early, so it's not easy for us, but we believed in ourselves and changed the game around."

schema.headline: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
description: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what ap
body: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening.""I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film."The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody."Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash."We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them."He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going."There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.   What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
